title: Relative clauses and embedded clauses

objectives.can: Mark where a relative or other subordinate clause begins and ends and say what it modifies.

explanation.summary: Long Greek sentences are built from clauses placed inside other clauses. A relative word (ὅς, ὅστις, ὅπου), a conjunction (ὅτε, ὡς, καθώς, ἕως, ὅτι, ἵνα) or a participle opens a subordinate clause, and the reader's task is to see where it begins, where it ends, and what it belongs to.

sections.heading: The relative clause
body: A relative clause is introduced by a relative pronoun and describes a noun that comes before it, the antecedent. In Acts 8:27, ἀνὴρ Αἰθίοψ εὐνοῦχος is followed by ὃς ἦν ἐπὶ πάσης τῆς γάζης αὐτῆς: 'who was over all her treasury'. The relative ὃς is masculine singular because the man is, and nominative because it is the subject of ἦν.

That is the general rule. The relative takes its gender and number from the antecedent, and its case from its own job in its own clause. In Matthew 2:9, ὁ ἀστὴρ ὃν εἶδον ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ, the relative ὃν is masculine singular like ἀστήρ, but accusative, because it is the object of εἶδον. The clause modifies 'the star' and ends at the end of its own verb phrase, before προῆγεν.

sections.heading: Other words that open subordinate clauses
body: A clause need not describe a noun. It may tell when, where, how, why or what. The words that open such clauses are mostly conjunctions or relative adverbs. The table lists the ones named in this lesson. The sense of each is a tendency; the context decides.

The words ὅτι and ἵνα each do more than one job. ὅτι may give a reason, or the content of what someone says or knows, as in 1 John 1:5, where ὅτι introduces the message. ἵνα may give a purpose, or the content of a command, as in John 13:34, where it follows ἐντολήν.

Kind of clause
Example
rows: relative: 'as many as, as much as'
ὅτι ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν, 1 John 1:5

sections.heading: The case of the relative: attraction
body: Now and then the relative does not take the case of its own clause but the case of its antecedent. Grammarians call this attraction. John 4:14 shows both patterns in one verse: ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος οὗ ἐγὼ δώσω αὐτῷ and then τὸ ὕδωρ ὃ δώσω αὐτῷ. In both clauses the water is what is given. In the first, οὗ is genitive like ὕδατος, because of attraction; in the second, ὃ is accusative, the ordinary case for the object of δώσω.

Ephesians 1:6, ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς, is commonly explained in the same way: ἧς takes the genitive of χάριτος although a verb of favouring would otherwise call for the accusative. A related pattern is Luke 1:4, περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων, where the antecedent noun λόγων has moved inside the relative clause and ὧν agrees with it. If a relative has a case you cannot explain from its own clause, look for an antecedent whose case it has borrowed.

sections.heading: When the antecedent is missing or comes later
body: Some relative clauses have no antecedent in front of them. They then act as a noun: 'the one who ...' or 'those who ...'. In John 1:12, ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν is the group that received him, and the αὐτοῖς in the next clause picks it up again as the people to whom he gave authority. The relative ὅς with ἄν often means 'whoever', as in John 4:14, ὃς δ' ἂν πίῃ.

1 John 1:1 is a more extreme case. It begins with a series of relative clauses, Ὃ ἦν ἀπ' ἀρχῆς, ὃ ἀκηκόαμεν, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν, ὃ ἐθεασάμεθα. All of them are neuter singular and mean 'that which ...'. Verse 2 interrupts with a parenthesis about the life that was shown, and verse 3 takes the relatives up again, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν καὶ ἀκηκόαμεν ἀπαγγέλλομεν, which supplies the verb they depend on. A reader has to keep the relatives open and carry them forward.

sections.heading: Marking the edges of a clause
body: A method for finding the edges. Find each finite verb. Each one belongs to its own clause. Next, find the word that opens the clause: a relative, a conjunction, or a participle. Then read forward until you reach the next opener or the next finite verb of a clause of the same level. Matthew 2:9 can be divided like this: the main clause is οἱ δὲ ἀκούσαντες τοῦ βασιλέως ἐπορεύθησαν, καὶ ἰδοὺ ὁ ἀστὴρ … προῆγεν αὐτούς; inside it, a relative clause ὃν εἶδον ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ; then a time clause ἕως ἐλθὼν ἐστάθη ἐπάνω, and inside that a place clause οὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον.

Different readers may draw an edge in a different place, particularly where a participle or a second relative could belong to either of two verbs. The sentence is the guide. Ask what each clause modifies, and prefer the nearest word that makes good sense.

misunderstandings: Giving the relative pronoun the case of its antecedent. The case comes from the relative's own clause, apart from the cases of attraction.
Treating ὅτι as always 'because'. After verbs of saying, knowing and seeing it often introduces what is said, known or seen.
Translating ὅστις as no different from ὅς. It is often general ('anyone who'), although the line is not firm in the New Testament.
Closing a clause too early. A subordinate clause can contain a participle, an infinitive or another clause, and the first verb you see is not always its last word.

deeper.heading: Ephesians 1:3–14
body: In this edition of the Greek text, Ephesians 1:3–14 runs as a single sentence, with no full stop before verse 14. Its clauses are strung together by relatives (ἧς, ᾧ, ὅ), prepositional phrases and participles. English translations usually break it into several sentences. A reader of the Greek does well to mark each relative and to ask what noun it takes up from the clause before.

deeper.heading: The word ὅστις
body: ὅστις is made, in origin, from the relative ὅς and the indefinite τις. In classical Greek it is usually general: 'whoever, anyone who'. In the New Testament it is still often general, as in Matthew 7:24, but it is sometimes used where plain ὅς would do. Grammarians draw the line in different places, so treat 'general' as the first thing to try, not as a rule.

examples.analysis: The main clause is about the star: ὁ ἀστὴρ … προῆγεν αὐτούς. ὃν εἶδον ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ is a relative clause modifying ἀστήρ; ὃν is masculine singular like its antecedent and accusative because it is the object of εἶδον. ἕως opens a time clause, 'until', with the participle ἐλθών and the verb ἐστάθη. Inside it, οὗ ἦν τὸ παιδίον is a place clause: 'where the child was'. A clause within a clause within a sentence.

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. examples.analysis: ὃς δ' ἂν πίῃ opens the sentence with a relative that has no antecedent: 'whoever drinks'. Then comes ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος οὗ ἐγὼ δώσω αὐτῷ, where οὗ is genitive like ὕδατος (attraction). A few words later, τὸ ὕδωρ ὃ δώσω αὐτῷ has the relative ὃ in the accusative, the object of δώσω. Both clauses say that the water is what is given.

quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. examples.analysis: Πᾶς … ὅστις ἀκούει … καὶ ποιεῖ opens with a general relative: 'everyone who hears and does'. The main verb is ὁμοιωθήσεται, with the dative ἀνδρὶ φρονίμῳ. The second ὅστις begins a relative clause that modifies ἀνδρί: 'a sensible man who built his house on the rock'. The first relative goes with Πᾶς, the second with ἀνδρί.

examples.analysis: The main clause is ἐντολὴν καινὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν. The first ἵνα clause, ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους, gives the content of the commandment. Next comes καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς, a comparison: 'just as I loved you'. The second ἵνα clause repeats the commandment, with καὶ ὑμεῖς: 'that you also love one another'. The sentence has one main verb and three subordinate clauses of different kinds.

examples.analysis: ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς is a relative clause modifying χάριτος. The relative is genitive singular feminine like its antecedent, and it is commonly explained as attracted from the accusative, the case a verb of favouring would otherwise give. ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ, with a perfect participle used as a noun, closes the clause. The sentence of which this verse is a part goes on in the next verses with a new relative, ἐν ᾧ.

practice.prompt: ὁ ἀστὴρ ὃν εἶδον ἐν τῇ ἀνατολῇ προῆγεν αὐτούς. What is the antecedent of ὃν (word 10), and why is it accusative?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: ἀστήρ; ὃν is accusative because it is the object of εἶδον
ἀνατολῇ; ὃν is accusative because it follows ἐν
αὐτούς; ὃν is accusative because it is the object of προῆγεν
ἀστήρ; ὃν is accusative because the antecedent is accusative
practice.explain: The relative is masculine singular like ἀστήρ. The antecedent is nominative, so case is not copied from it. ὃν is accusative because it is the object of εἶδον in the relative clause.

practice.prompt: ἀνὴρ Αἰθίοψ εὐνοῦχος … ὃς ἦν ἐπὶ πάσης τῆς γάζης αὐτῆς, ὃς ἐληλύθει προσκυνήσων εἰς Ἰερουσαλήμ. How many relative clauses are there, and what do they describe?

quoted.title: Acts
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: One, describing Candace
Two, one describing Candace and one describing Jerusalem
Two, both describing the Ethiopian man
None; the participle is the only subordinate clause
practice.explain: Each ὃς opens a relative clause, with its own finite verb (ἦν, ἐληλύθει). Both are masculine singular nominative, and both describe the man: he was over the treasury, and he had come to worship.

practice.prompt: ταῦτα ἐν Βηθανίᾳ ἐγένετο πέραν τοῦ Ἰορδάνου, ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης βαπτίζων. What does the clause ὅπου ἦν ὁ Ἰωάννης βαπτίζων do?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. options: It gives a purpose of the events
It describes the place: 'where John was baptising'
It is the main clause of the sentence
It gives a reason for the events
practice.explain: ὅπου is a relative adverb meaning 'where'. The clause has its own verb ἦν with the participle βαπτίζων (a periphrastic imperfect) and gives more about the place named before it.

practice.prompt: ἐντολὴν καινὴν δίδωμι ὑμῖν ἵνα ἀγαπᾶτε ἀλλήλους, καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς. What does καθὼς ἠγάπησα ὑμᾶς do?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It says when: 'when I loved you'
It is the content of the commandment
It says how, or in what way: 'just as I loved you'
It describes the noun ἐντολήν as a relative clause
practice.explain: καθώς opens a clause of comparison. The content of the commandment is the ἵνα clause before it. Time is not the main sense, and the clause has no relative pronoun.

check.prompt: Πᾶς οὖν ὅστις ἀκούει μου τοὺς λόγους τούτους καὶ ποιεῖ αὐτούς, ὁμοιωθήσεται ἀνδρὶ φρονίμῳ, ὅστις ᾠκοδόμησεν αὐτοῦ τὴν οἰκίαν. What does the second ὅστις clause (from word 14) modify?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: λόγους, the words
Πᾶς, the one who hears
ἀνδρί, the sensible man
ὁμοιωθήσεται, the verb
check.explain: The clause is a relative one and describes the nearest noun that fits: the man who built his house. The first ὅστις goes with Πᾶς. The second does not go back to it.

check.prompt: ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος οὗ ἐγὼ δώσω αὐτῷ … τὸ ὕδωρ ὃ δώσω αὐτῷ. Why are οὗ and ὃ in different cases when they refer to the same thing?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: Because the writer made a mistake
Because ὃ is the object of δώσω, as expected, and οὗ is genitive by attraction to ὕδατος
Because the two clauses have different verbs
Because οὗ is plural and ὃ is singular
check.explain: Both would normally be accusative, the object of δώσω. In the first clause the relative has been drawn into the genitive of its antecedent ὕδατος, which follows ἐκ. The verbs are the same, and both pronouns are singular.

check.prompt: ἕως ἂν παρέλθῃ ὁ οὐρανὸς καὶ ἡ γῆ, ἰῶτα ἓν ἢ μία κεραία οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου. What does the clause that begins ἕως ἂν (word 4) do?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It is a relative clause that modifies οὐρανός
It is a time clause, 'until heaven and earth pass away', that modifies οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ
It is a purpose clause: 'in order that heaven pass away'
It is the content clause of a verb of saying
check.explain: ἕως ἂν with the subjunctive opens a clause of time, 'until'. It is subordinate to the main verb of the other half of the sentence, οὐ μὴ παρέλθῃ, a strong denial. The second ἕως ἂν clause, near the end, is a time clause of the same kind. It has no relative pronoun, so it does not modify a noun.

check.prompt: ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου, ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου. Which words make the subordinate clause?

quoted.title: Matthew
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: None: the sentence has only one clause
καὶ ἡ καρδία σου only
ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου
ὅπου γάρ ἐστιν ὁ θησαυρός σου
check.explain: ὅπου opens a place clause with its own verb ἐστιν. The main clause is ἐκεῖ ἔσται καὶ ἡ καρδία σου, in which ἐκεῖ picks up the ὅπου: 'where ..., there ...'. γάρ is a connective, taken up in a later lesson, and does not belong to the pattern.

check.prompt: ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν, ἔδωκεν αὐτοῖς ἐξουσίαν τέκνα θεοῦ γενέσθαι. What is the role of ὅσοι δὲ ἔλαβον αὐτόν?

quoted.title: John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: It is a conditional clause with ἐάν
It is a time clause: 'when he received'
It is a relative clause without an antecedent, 'as many as received him', picked up by αὐτοῖς
It is a purpose clause
check.explain: ὅσοι means 'as many as'. The group is the subject of ἔλαβον, and in the main clause αὐτοῖς refers back to it as the people to whom he gave authority.

check.prompt: ἵνα ἐπιγνῷς περὶ ὧν κατηχήθης λόγων τὴν ἀσφάλειαν. What is the case and gender of ὧν (word 3), and what does it agree with?

quoted.title: Luke
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: Dative singular, agreeing with περί
Genitive plural masculine, agreeing with λόγων, which stands inside the relative clause
Nominative singular masculine, agreeing with ἀσφάλειαν
Accusative plural, agreeing with ἐπιγνῷς
check.explain: ὧν is genitive plural, the case that περί takes here, and agrees with the noun λόγων, which has been moved into the relative clause. ἀσφάλειαν is feminine, and ἐπιγνῷς is a verb.

check.prompt: Ὃ ἦν ἀπ’ ἀρχῆς, ὃ ἀκηκόαμεν, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν … These relative clauses (1 John 1:1) have no noun before them. How should they be read?

quoted.title: 1 John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: As a single clause with the main verb ἦν
As three separate sentences with no link
As questions, because they have no antecedent
As a series of neuter relatives, 'that which …', that wait for a main verb that comes later in the passage
check.explain: Each ὅ is neuter singular and begins a relative clause with its own verb. Verse 2 interrupts with a parenthesis, and verse 3 takes the relatives up again, ὃ ἑωράκαμεν καὶ ἀκηκόαμεν ἀπαγγέλλομεν, which supplies the verb they depend on.

check.prompt: εἰς ἔπαινον δόξης τῆς χάριτος αὐτοῦ ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ. What does the relative clause ἧς ἐχαρίτωσεν ἡμᾶς modify?

quoted.title: Ephesians
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: ἔπαινον, 'praise'
χάριτος, 'grace'
ἠγαπημένῳ, 'the beloved'
ἡμᾶς, 'us'
check.explain: ἧς is feminine singular genitive, so its antecedent is a feminine singular noun in the genitive: χάριτος. ἔπαινον is masculine, and ἠγαπημένῳ is dative.

check.prompt: Καὶ ἔστιν αὕτη ἡ ἀγγελία ἣν ἀκηκόαμεν ἀπ' αὐτοῦ καὶ ἀναγγέλλομεν ὑμῖν, ὅτι ὁ θεὸς φῶς ἐστιν. What does ὅτι introduce?

quoted.title: 1 John
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: The content of the message (ἀγγελία): 'that God is light'
A time: 'when God is light'
A reason: 'because we heard it'
A place: 'where God is light'
check.explain: ἡ ἀγγελία is first described by the relative clause ἣν ἀκηκόαμεν …, and then ὅτι tells what the message is. A reason is possible for ὅτι in general, but here the message and its content go together.

check.prompt: ἐν ᾧ ἔχομεν τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν διὰ τοῦ αἵματος αὐτοῦ. What does ᾧ (word 1) refer back to?

quoted.title: Ephesians
quoted.credit: Greek text: SBL Greek New Testament (SBLGNT), Society of Biblical Literature and Logos Bible Software, CC BY 4.0. Morphology and lemmas: MorphGNT SBLGNT edition, James K. Tauber, CC BY-SA 3.0. Glosses: Dodson Greek Lexicon (public domain). Strong's numbers: Strong's Greek Dictionary, Open Scriptures JSON edition.

options: αἵματος, because it is in the same verse
τὴν ἀπολύτρωσιν, which follows it
Nothing: ᾧ is a conjunction meaning 'and'
A noun in the previous verse: the clause begins a new relative clause linked to the phrase before it
check.explain: ᾧ is a relative pronoun, dative singular, after ἐν. Its antecedent is in the previous verse, where ἐν τῷ ἠγαπημένῳ ends the earlier clause, and the new clause carries the sentence on. ἀπολύτρωσιν is accusative and cannot be its antecedent.

reading.why: Relative clauses in every verse, from the long series of ὅ in verse 1 to ἣν ἀκηκόαμεν and the ὅτι clause in verse 5. The sentence begun in verse 1 is interrupted in verse 2 and resumed in verse 3.
